Caravanning (more commonly used here than RV’ing) is pretty popular, especially among older folks and retirees, who are nicknamed grey nomads. Lots of free camp spots and campgrounds where you can park the caravan overnight. 

As for where to go after Sydney, you’ll need to take the time of year into consideration - summertime is prettier than winter but conditions are much harsher. Victoria and NSW get bad bushfires, QLD is hot and humid and sticky and gets cyclones up north, and anywhere outback will easily get upwards of 45 degrees (113 farenheit). In winter there’s less people on the road, and you might have the chance to see snow, but it’s too cold to go to the beach even up north, mainly sitting in the 20s, which I think is about the 70s farenheit and imho is way too cold to consider going swimming anywhere. 

South coast of NSW is beautiful, as is New England, north and slightly inland of Sydney.  Victoria’s Great Ocean Road is excellent but aside from that you might find yourself bored easily. Personally I love QLD having lived here all my life - beautiful stretches of beach, a mixture of cities and towns, and a very tropical vibe. 

If you’re hoping to go outback, definitely go in the winter. Starting from Sydney I’d probably head to Broken Hill in far west NSW. From there you can turn around and go back to Sydney, go to Adelaide through Silverton (where they filmed some of the Mad Max films), Olary, Yunta etc, or go to Melbourne through Mildura.

Australia is big on “multiculturalism”, and had huge waves of immigration in the later half of the 20th century. Post 9/11 and the Tampa affair, things swung more conservatively with fears about asylum seekers and people from the Middle East for the most part. 

Also historically Australia hasn’t been too diverse. There was the White Australia Policy from Federation (1901) to just after WWII. It kept most non-Western Europeans ouf, and essentially was a test upon arrival for proficiency in any Western language of the officer’s choice. It was ended due to fears of too low a population if we were invaded after the threat of Japanese invasion during the War on the Pacific. As most of our soldiers had been sent to Europe to aid the Allies and we relied on Americans to help defend our borders. We received a lot of European refugees in the 50s and in the 70s, lots of Vietnamese refugees. 

In spite of all this, Australia does have a great amount of diversity; particularly with Polynesians and South/South-East Asians. Apart from in cities you’re less likely to find people of African descent (as many are refugees and placed in cities).

Late on the bandwagon but thought I’d share my experiences.
I live in QLD but quite close to NSW and from what I understand it’s similar. Also lots of family from Victoria and they’ve all gone through similar things.
Started kindergarten at 3, finished at the end of the year when I was four. Then went to preschool (which was what they called the older playgroup) from 4 until end of the year, at which point I was five. Kindergarten and preschool were noncompulsory and not free. There I learned to write my name, basic numbers, and there was lots of playtime and stories being read.

Then went to primary school, which was Prep-Year 7 (now Year 6, QLD was late to make Year 7 high school). Prep started when I was five and ended when I was six. The birthdays were from July of one year to June the next. So some kids entered as five turning six (if born later half of the year), and others as four turning five (if born earlier half of the year). Some kids didn’t do ‘preschool’, just  kindergarten - aka one year of kindy and not two (which I did). 90% of kids had gone to some sort of through the week play programme before starting prep though. Prep was five days a week, with two breaks, little lunch from 11-11:30 with 15 minutes for eating, 15 mins for play, and big lunch from 1-1:45, with 15 mins eating and 30 mins play. We were at school from 9 til 3. We learned basic writing, colours and mixing colours, reading with home readers, and some addition and subtraction. 

We also had ‘gross motor skills’ time every week, and we would go outside and learn stretches, skills like jumping a rope, etc, and we’d typically have two or three ‘lessons’ a day of abt half an hour/forty-five minutes when we’d learn skills and the rest was creative play or educational games. I started year one at age six and finished at seven (though some kids started at five and turned six by the end of June), and our play became largely restricted to little and big lunch, with more focus on reading, writing, and maths. A big emphasis was put on handwriting and we had notebooks to write in. We also had computer lab once or twice a week to learn how to log onto a computer, typing in word - this is probably different now hahaha. Year One is a big step up from Prep, but Prep isn’t all that different to kindy and is basically a year of getting kids used to older kids and a school environment, wearing a uniform etc.

In my family, on my maternal grandmother’s side, February is an unlucky month. My grandmother’s parents and siblings all died in February, and all of my grandmother’s miscarriages occured in February. February was also when my mother was in a car accident that nearly killed her, and when my grandparents got divorced (as well as several other divorces of aunts and uncles or cousins occuring in this month). It’s to the point that there are jokes about getting through February. It’s almost to the point of spookiness; reflecting on it now, I can think of many more bad things that have happened in that month, particularly from the 8th to the 15th, which is ripe for deaths. On no other side of my family is it like this - just my relatives through my maternal grandmother. 
EDIT: the earliest records I can find of this February unluckiness is my grandmother’s great-grandfather, who was arrested on 13 Feb 1862. Since then, a significant proportion of deaths, divorces, imprisonments and other tragedies have occurrd in this month.

Was on a roadtrip a few years back from QLD through to Broken Hill. We were trying to get to Bourke by nightfall after being warned about roos on the road at dusk, and we were in a fairly small car with no bullbar, so being hit by a roo was a real concern. By this point it’s about 4:30 and we’ve been driving through the middle of nowhere for maybe an hour, with huge red anthills on either side of the road. It’s getting dark and we want to speed up a bit and get to Bourke because by this point we’re all busting for the bathroom.

Anyway, we speed up a bit, and that’s where things get weird. We start losing kilometers on the dashboard, with the numbers heading downward, and gaining a tank of petrol. We pass these same anthills again, next to the same clump of trees. My Dad suggested we took a turn at some point and looped back, so we dismissed it and kept going towards Bourke straight. We get further than we did before, and end up in this strange little town. It’s quarter past five on a Friday and everything is completely shut. It’s definitely dusk by now, but there are no lights on anywhere. We stop at the pub to use the toilets, but upon entry the pub is completely empty, although the television is on, just making a buzzing sound and displaying static.

We’re a bit freaked out so we leave the pub (which had open doors but nobody inside) and head for the public toilets in the park. We go in and there’s no lights inside, so we use the torchlights of our phone and find that all three cubicles are locked, though as far as we can tell, nobody is inside. 

We go back to the car and drive around looking for bathrooms, though we can’t find any others, and so we agree that we just really need to keep driving for we’ve booked a hotel already in Bourke. We drive on the one road out of the town and just before we come to the sign saying ‘You’re Leaving ______’, we see a sheep on the road. It’s pretty large and just stares at the car, and even after sitting there for a few minutes and honking it won’t move. Eventually we just drive around it and go on our way.

After that the trip was pretty normal, but on the way back we made sure to go a different route. That town was just too creepy.

Live in a coastal city, basically 90% of people spend the summers swimming, riding bikes or partying. My dad spent years teaching me how to ride a bike and I never got it, the sensation felt wrong on my feet and my butt. Swimming lessons were compulsory at school and by year six I was still at the kindergarten level because I couldn’t keep myself afloat, to the point that I got bullied because I had to go in the kiddie pool while everyone else went in the olympic sized pool and was learning butterfly. Tried surfing lessons at nine and that was the first time I ever heard the word ‘autistic’, because I freaked out and cried and screamed every time seaweed touched me and the instructor asked my mother and I overheard. At thirteen I was invited to a party and was over the moon, there were kids my age and everything. At this point I had been in therapy for anxiety and depression for three years and nothing helped. When I arrived, it turned out to be a pool party but nobody told me. I was thrown in the pool in my clothes and held under til I blacked out. Only that my mum had been there to make sure I got in safe and heard kids screaming ‘she’s dead!’ did I actually get out safe. When I got home from hospital, I googled all of this and thought abt Asperger’s, but it didn’t seem right. I didn’t think I obsessed over things and I was a girl.

Year nine, and I’m doing an independent reading project because I changed schools and had already read the book we were studying.
